subsection.title: Delta as a response
subsection.p: The Greek letter \delta, pronounced delta, will represent the allowed input error.
To say that x is within \delta of a, but not equal to a, means

subsection.p: The order matters: first comes \varepsilon, then we choose \delta.
The value of \delta is allowed to depend on \varepsilon. Usually, smaller \varepsilon requires smaller \delta.

The definition in one sentence. The limit of f(x) as x\to a is L if every output window around L contains all nearby values f(x), once x is restricted to a small enough punctured input window around a.

subsection.title: Why the point x=a is excluded
subsection.p: The condition 0\lt |x-a| is not a technical nuisance. It preserves the meaning of a limit.
Recall the function
We know that \lim_{x\to 1}F(x)=3, even though F(1)=-1.
If the definition forced us to check x=1, then the output error from 3 would be
For \varepsilon=1, this would fail. But that failure should not destroy the limit, because a limit is about nearby values.
The puncture 0\lt |x-a| lets the limit ignore the value at a.
Limits are local around the point, not necessarily at the point.

subsection.title: Proving simple limits
subsection.p: An \varepsilon-\delta proof often begins by working backward.
We ask: What condition on |x-a| would force |f(x)-L|\lt \varepsilon?
Then we choose \delta to guarantee that condition.

statement.p: We need to make |(2x+5)-11|\lt \varepsilon. Simplify the error:
So it is enough to require 2|x-3|\lt \varepsilon, that is, |x-3|\lt \frac{\varepsilon}{2}. This tells us what to choose: \delta=\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.

subsection.p: The proof does not say that x is close to 3 in vague language. It gives a rule. If the requested output error is \varepsilon, then the input error \delta=\varepsilon/2 is enough.

statement.p: The factor |x-2| is the input error. The other factor, |x+2|, must be controlled.
If x is close to 2, then x+2 is close to 4. We only need a simple bound, not a perfect one. Require |x-2|\lt 1. Then 1\lt x\lt 3, so 3\lt x+2\lt 5. Thus |x+2|\lt 5.
To make this less than \varepsilon, it is enough to require 5|x-2|\lt \varepsilon, or |x-2|\lt \frac{\varepsilon}{5}.
We need both requirements: |x-2|\lt 1 and |x-2|\lt \frac{\varepsilon}{5}. So choose the smaller of the two: \delta=\min\left(1,\frac{\varepsilon}{5}\right).

subsection.p: This proof shows a common pattern. We first restrict x to a simple neighborhood of a so that the extra factors stay bounded. Then we choose a smaller \delta if needed to meet the desired error.

subsection.p: There are two important details.
First, the horizontal band is chosen first. That is the \varepsilon-challenge.
Second, the vertical strip may depend on the horizontal band. A thinner output band usually requires a thinner input strip.

statement.p: Suppose, for contradiction, that the limit were some number L. Choose \varepsilon=\frac{1}{2}.
No matter how small \delta\gt 0 is, both numbers x=\frac{\delta}{2} and x=-\frac{\delta}{2} satisfy 0\lt |x|\lt \delta.
The first inequality says \frac{1}{2}\lt L\lt \frac{3}{2}. The second says -\frac{3}{2}\lt L\lt -\frac{1}{2}. No number L can lie in both intervals. Therefore no two-sided limit exists.
This is the precise version of the picture: the two sides approach different targets.

This is why the function J(x)=\frac{|x|}{x} has one-sided limits at 0. From the left it is always -1, and from the right it is always 1. The one-sided tests pass separately, but the two-sided test fails because one \delta-window must handle both sides at once.

subsection.title: What the definition gives us
subsection.p: The precise definition is not meant to replace intuition. It protects intuition.

It explains why a table can suggest a limit but not prove it. It explains why the value at the point may not matter. It explains why a jump breaks a two-sided limit. It gives us a way to prove limit laws instead of trusting them from graphs.
Most of the time, we will calculate limits using algebra, known limit laws, and continuity. But the \varepsilon-\delta definition is the foundation underneath those shortcuts.

principle.title: What a finite limit really says

statement.p: The statement \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L means that output error can be forced below any chosen tolerance by making input error small enough, while not requiring x=a.

subsection.p: Now that limits have a precise meaning, we can define a special kind of well-behaved function. It is the case where the nearby limit and the actual value agree. That property is called continuity, and it is the reason many familiar graphs can be drawn without lifting the pencil.
